blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's recall.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous standard you have learnt the following constructions.
Let us recall those constructions.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ To construct a line parallel to a given line and passing through a
given point outside the line.
$\bullet$ To construct the perpendicular bisector of a given line segment.
$\bullet$ To construct a triangle whose sides are given.
$\bullet$ To divide a given line segment into given number of equal parts
$\bullet$ To divide a line segment in the given ratio.
$\bullet$ To construct an angle congruent to the given angle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the ninth standard you have carried out the activity of preparing a map of
surroundings of your school. Before constructing a building we make its plan. The
surroundings of a school and its map, the building and its plan are similar to each
other. We need to draw similar figures in Geography, architecture, machine drawing
etc. A triangle is the simplest closed figure. We shall learn how to construct a triangle
similar to the given triangle.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Construction of Similar Triangle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To construct a triangle similar to the given triangle, satisfying the condition of
given ratio of corresponding sides.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The corresponding sides of similar triangles are in the same proportion and the
corresponding angles of these triangles are equal. Using this property, a triangle which
is similar to the given triangle can be constructed.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (1) $\Delta$ ABC $\sim$ $\Delta$ PQR, in $\Delta$ ABC, AB = 5.4 cm, BC = 4.2 cm, AC = 6.0 cm.
AB: PQ = 3:2. Construct $\Delta$ ABC and $\Delta$ PQR.

Rough Figure

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\Delta$ ABC and $\Delta$ PQR are similar.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ their corresponding sides are proportional.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{PQ}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{QR}} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{PR}} = \frac{3}{2} \dots\dots\dots\dots (\mathrm{I}) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As the sides AB, BC, AC are known, we can find the lengths of sides
PQ, QR, PR.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using equation [I]

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{5.4}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{4.2}{\text{QR}} = \frac{6.0}{\text{PR}} = \frac{3}{2} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore PQ = 3.6 \text{ cm}, QR = 2.8 \text{ cm and PR} = 4.0 \text{ cm}$

**For More Information**
While drawing the triangle similar to the given triangle, sometimes the lengths
of the sides we obtain by calculation are not easily measureable by a scale. In such
a situation we can use the construction ‘To divide the given segment in the given
number of equaul parts’.
For example, if length of side AB is $\frac{11.6}{3}$ cm, then by dividing the line segment
of length 11.6 cm in three equal parts, we can draw segment AB.

blocks.text:
If we know the lengths of all sides of $\Delta$ PQR, we can construct $\Delta$ PQR.
In the above example (1) there was no common vertex in the given triangle and
the triangle to be constructed. If there is a common vertex, it is convenient to follow
the method in the following example.

**Ex.**(2) Construct any $\Delta$ ABC. Construct $\Delta$ A'BC' such that AB : A'B = 5:3 and
$\Delta$ ABC $\sim$ $\Delta$ A'BC'
**Analysis :** As shown in fig 4.3 , let the points B, A, A' and
B, C, C' be collinear.
$\Delta$ ABC $\sim$ $\Delta$ A'BC' $\therefore$ $\angle$ ABC = $\angle$A'BC'
$\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{A'B}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{BC}'} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{A'C}'} = \frac{5}{3}$
Rough Figure

$\therefore$ the length of side BC' will be equal to 3 parts out of 5 equal parts of side
BC. So if we construct $\Delta$ ABC, point C' will be on the side BC, at a distance
equal to 3 parts from B. Now A' is the point of intersection of AB and a line
through C', parallel to CA.

blocks.text: \textbf{Ex. (3)}   Construct $\Delta$ A'BC' similar to $\Delta$ ABC such that AB:A'B = 5:7

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**EX. (3)** Construct $\Delta A$ BC similar to $\Delta ABC$ such that $AB:A B = 5:7$
**Analysis :** Let points $B, A, A'$ as well as points $B, C, C'$ be collinear.
$\Delta ABC \sim \Delta A'BC'$ and $AB : A'B = 5:7$
$\therefore$ sides of $\Delta ABC$ are smaller than sides of $\Delta A'BC'$
and $\angle ABC \cong \angle A'BC'$
Let us draw a rough figure with these
considerations. Now $\frac{BC}{BC'} = \frac{5}{7}$
$\therefore$ If $\sec BC$ is divided into 5 equal parts, then $\sec BC'$ will be 7 times each
part of $\sec BC$.
$\therefore$ let us divide side BC of $\Delta ABC$ in 5 equal parts and locate point $C'$ at a
distance equal to 7 such parts from $B$ on ray $BC$. A line through point $C'$
parallel to $\sec AC$ is drawn it will intersect ray $BA$ at point $A'$. According
to the basic proportionality theorem we will get $\Delta A'BC'$ as described.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of construction :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) Construct any $\Delta$ ABC.
(2) Divide segment BC into 5 five equal parts. Fix point $C'$ on ray BC such that length
of $BC'$ is seven times of each equal part of seg BC
(3) Draw a line parallel to side AC, through $C'$. Name the point of intersection of the
line and ray BA as $A'$.
We get the required $\Delta$ $A'BC'$ similar to $\Delta$ ABC.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Construction of a tangent to a circle at a point on the circle

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: (i) Using the centre of the circle.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Analysis :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose we want to construct a tangent $l$ passing through a point P on the
circle with centre C. We shall use the property that a line perpendicular to the
radius at its outer end is a tangent to the
circle. If CP is a radius with point P on the
circle, line $l$ through P and perpendicular
to CP is the tangent at P. For this we
will use the construction of drawing a
perpendicular to a line through a point on it.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 4.9

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: For convenience we shall draw ray CP

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of construction

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) Draw a circle with centre C.
Take any point P on the circle.
(2) Draw ray CP.
(3) Draw line $l$ perpendicular to
ray CX through point P.
Line $l$ is the required tangent to
the circle at point 'P'.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: ii) Without using the centre of the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Example:** Construct a circle of any radius. Take any point C on it. Construct a
tangent to the circle without using centre of the circle.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Analysis :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As shown in the figure, let line $l$ be the
tangent to the circle at point C. Line CB is
a chord and $\angle$ CAB is an inscribed angle.
Now by tangent- secant angle theorem,
$\angle CAB \cong \angle BCD$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
By converse of tangent- secant theorem, if we draw the line CD such that,
$\angle CAB \cong \angle BCD$, then it will be the required tangent.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of Construction :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) Draw a circle of a suitable radius. Take any point C on it.
(2) Draw chord CB and an inscribed $\angle CAB$ .

(3) With the centre A and any
convenient radius draw an arc
intersecting the sides of $\angle BAC$
in points M and N.
(4) Using the same radius and centre
C, draw an arc intersecting the
chord CB at point R.

(5) Taking the radius equal to d(MN) and centre R, draw an arc intersecting the
arc drawn in the previous step. Let D be the point of intersection of these
arcs. Draw line CD. Line CD is the required tangent to the circle.

Note that $\angle MAN$ and $\angle BCD$ in the above figure are congruent. If we draw
seg MN and seg RD, then $\Delta MAN$ and $\Delta RCD$ are congruent by SSS test.

$\therefore \angle MAN \cong \angle BCD$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: To construct tangents to a circle from a point outside the circle.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Analysis :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As shown in the figure let P be a point in
the exterior of the circle. Let PA and PB
be the tangents to the circle with the centre
O, touching the circle in points A and B
respectively. So if we find points A and B
on the circle, we can construct the
tangents PA and PB. If OA and OB are
the radii of the circle, then OA $\perp$ line PA
and seg OB $\perp$ line PB.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\Delta$ OAP and OBP are right angled triangles and seg OP is their common
hypotenuse. If we draw a circle with diameter OP, then the points where it intersects
the circle with centre O, will be the positions of points A and B respectively, because
angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Steps of Construction

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) Construct a circle of any radius with
centre O.
(2) Take any point P in the exterior of the
circle.
(3) Draw segment OP. Draw perpendicular
bisector of seg OP to get its midpoint M.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(4) Draw a circle with radius OM and centre M                                     **Fig. 4.**
(5) Name the points of intersection of the two circles as A and B.
(6) Draw line PA and line PB.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: 5 Co-ordinate Geometry

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's study.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: $\bullet$ Distance formula $\quad \bullet$ Section formula $\quad \bullet$ Slope of a line

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's recall.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We know how to find the distance between any two points on a number line.
If co-ordinates of points $P,Q$ and $R$ are $-1,-5$ and $4$ respectively then find the
length of $\sec PQ$, $\sec QR$.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 5.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the co-ordinates of points A and B and $x_2 > x_1$ then length of
seg AB = d(A,B) = $x_2 - x_1$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As shown in the figure, co-ordinates of points P,Q and R are $-1,-5$ and $4$
respectively.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\therefore \quad \mathrm{d}(\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}) = (-1) - (-5) = -1 + 5 = 4$
and $\quad \mathrm{d}(\mathrm{Q}, \mathrm{R}) = 4 - (-5) = 4 + 5 = 9$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Using the same concept we can find the distance between two points on the
same axis in XY-plane.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(1) To find distance between any two points on an axis .
Two points on an axis are like two points on the number line. Note
that points on the X-axis have co-ordinates such as $(2, 0)$, $\left(\frac{-5}{2}, 0\right)$,
$(8, 0)$. Similarly points on the Y-axis have co-ordinates such as $(0, 1)$, $\left(0, \frac{17}{2}\right)$,
$(0, -3)$. Part of the X-axis which shows negative co-ordinates is OX'
and part of the Y-axis which shows negative co-ordinates is OY'.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
i) To find distance between two
points on X-axis.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 5.2

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the above figure, points
A($x_1$, 0 ) and B($x_2$, 0) are on
X- axis such that, $x_2 > x_1$
$\therefore$ d(A, B) = $x_2 - x_1$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
ii) To find distance between two
points on Y-axis.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 5.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the above figure, points
$P(0, y_1)$ and $Q(0, y_2)$ are on
$Y-$ axis such that, $y_2 > y_1$
$\therefore d(P,Q) = y_2 - y_1$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(2) To find the distance between two points if the segment joining these points is
parallel to any axis in the XY plane.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 5.4

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
i) In the figure, seg AB is parallel to
X- axis.
$\therefore$ $y$ co-ordinates of points A and B
are equal
Draw seg AL and seg BM
perpendicular to X-axis
$\therefore$ $\square$ ABML is a rectangle.
$\therefore$ AB = LM
But, LM = $x_2$ - $x_1$
$\therefore$ d(A,B) = $x_2$ - $x_1$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 5.5

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
ii) In the figure seg PQ is parallel to
Y- axis.
$\therefore$ $x$ co-ordinates of points P and Q
are equal
Draw seg PR and seg QS
perpendicular to Y-axis.
$\therefore$ $\square$PQSR is a rectangle
$\therefore$ PQ = RS
But, RS = $y_2$ - $y_1$
$\therefore$ d(P,Q) = $y_2$ - $y_1$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Activity:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the figure, $\sec$ AB $\parallel$ Y-axis and
$\sec$ CB $\parallel$ X-axis. Co-ordinates of
points A and C are given.
To find AC, fill in the boxes given below.
$\Delta$ ABC is a right angled triangle.
According to Pythagoras theorem,
$(AB)^2 + (BC)^2 = \square$
We will find co-ordinates of point B
to find the lengths AB and BC,
CB $\parallel$ X- axis $\therefore y$ co-ordinate of B = $\square$
BA $\parallel$ Y- axis $\therefore x$ co-ordinate of B = $\square$
AB = 3 - $\square$ = $\square$ BC = $\square$
$\therefore AC^2 = \square + \square = \square \quad \therefore AC =$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
CB || X- axis $\therefore$ $y$ co-ordinate of B = $\square$ \hfill \textbf{Fig. 5.6}

BA || Y- axis $\therefore$ $x$ co-ordinate of B = $\square$

AB = $\text{\textcircled{3}} - \text{\textcircled{1}} = \text{\textcircled{1}}$ \hfill BC = $\text{\textcircled{1}} - \text{\textcircled{1}} = \text{\textcircled{4}}$

$\therefore \text{AC}^2 = \text{\textcircled{1}} + \text{\textcircled{1}} = \text{\textcircled{1}}$ \hfill $\therefore \text{AC} = \text{\textcircled{1}}\sqrt{17}$

blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.text: Distance formula

blocks.label: Image-caption

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** Find the distance between the points $P(-1, 1)$ and $Q(5, -7)$.

**Solution** :Suppose co-ordinates of point $P$ are $(x_1, y_1)$ and of point $Q$ are $(x_2, y_2)$.
$$x_1 = -1, \quad y_1 = 1, \quad x_2 = 5, \quad y_2 = -7$$
According to distance formula, $d(P, Q) = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2}$
$$= \sqrt{[5 - (-1)]^2 + [(-7) - 1]^2}$$
$$= \sqrt{(6)^2 + (-8)^2}$$
$$= \sqrt{36 + 64}$$
$$d(P, Q) = \sqrt{100} = 10$$
$\therefore$ distance between points $P$ and $Q$ is $10$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (2)** Show that points $A(-3, 2)$, $B(1, -2)$ and $C(9, -10)$ are collinear.
**Solution** : If the sum of any two distances out of $d(A, B)$, $d(B, C)$ and $d(A, C)$ is
equal to the third , then the three points $A, B$ and $C$ are collinear.
$\therefore$ we will find $d(A, B)$, $d(B, C)$ and $d(A, C)$.
Co-ordinates of $A$      Co-ordinates of $B$      Distance formula
$(-3, 2)$                  $(1, -2)$                  $d(A,B) = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2 + (y_2-y_1)^2}$
$(x_1, y_1)$                  $(x_2, y_2)$
$\therefore d(A, B) = \sqrt{[1-(-3)]^2 + [(-2)-2]^2}$ ......... from distance formula
$= \sqrt{(1+3)^2 + (-4)^2}$
$= \sqrt{16+16}$
$= \sqrt{32} \quad = 4\sqrt{2}$ .........(I)
$d(B, C) = \sqrt{(9-1)^2 + (-10+2)^2}$
$= \sqrt{64+64} = 8\sqrt{2}$ .........(II)
and $d(A, C) = \sqrt{(9+3)^2 + (-10-2)^2}$
$= \sqrt{144+144} \quad = 12\sqrt{2}$ .........(III)
$\therefore$ from(I), (II) and (III)      $4\sqrt{2} + 8\sqrt{2} = 12\sqrt{2}$
$\therefore d(A, B) + d(B, C) = d(A, C)$
$\therefore$ Points $A, B, C$ are collinear.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (3)**   Verify, whether points $P(6, -6)$, $Q(3, -7)$ and $R(3, 3)$ are collinear.

**Solution :** $PQ = \sqrt{(6-3)^2 + (-6+7)^2}$      .........by distance formula

          $= \sqrt{(3)^2 + (1)^2}$      $= \sqrt{10}$      ......... (I)

        $QR = \sqrt{(3-3)^2 + (-7-3)^2}$

          $= \sqrt{(0)^2 + (-10)^2}$      $= \sqrt{100}$      ......... (II)

        $PR = \sqrt{(3-6)^2 + (3+6)^2}$

          $= \sqrt{(-3)^2 + (9)^2}$      $= \sqrt{90}$      ......... (III)

        From I, II and III out of $\sqrt{10}$, $\sqrt{100}$ and $\sqrt{90}$, $\sqrt{100}$ is the largest number.
        Now we will verify whether $(\sqrt{100})$ and $(\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{90})$ are equal.

        For this compare $(\sqrt{100})^2$ and $(\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{90})^2$ .

        You will see that $(\sqrt{10} + \sqrt{90}) > (\sqrt{100})$ $\therefore$ $PQ + PR \neq QR$

        $\therefore$ points $P(6, -6)$, $Q(3, -7)$ and $R(3, 3)$ are not collinear.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (4)** Show that points $(1, 7)$, $(4, 2)$, $(-1, -1)$ and $(-4, 4)$ are vertices of a square.
**Solution** : In a quadrilateral, if all sides are of equal length and both diagonals are
of equal length, then it is a square.
$\therefore$ we will find lengths of sides and diagonals by using the distance formula.
Suppose, $A(1, 7)$, $B(4, 2)$, $C(-1, -1)$ and $D(-4,4)$ are the given points.
$$AB = \sqrt{(1-4)^2 + (7-2)^2} \quad = \sqrt{9+25} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$BC = \sqrt{(4+1)^2 + (2+1)^2} \quad = \sqrt{25+9} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$CD = \sqrt{(-1+4)^2 + (-1-4)^2} \quad = \sqrt{9+25} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$DA = \sqrt{(1+4)^2 + (7-4)^2} \quad = \sqrt{25+9} = \sqrt{34}$$
$$AC = \sqrt{(1+1)^2 + (7+1)^2} \quad = \sqrt{4+64} = \sqrt{68}$$
$$BD = \sqrt{(4+4)^2 + (2-4)^2} \quad = \sqrt{64+4} = \sqrt{68}$$
$\therefore AB = BC = CD = DA$ and $AC = BD$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the lengths of four sides are equal and two diagonals are equal.
$\therefore (1,7), (4,2), (-1,-1)$ and $(-4,4)$ are the vertices of a square.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (5)**   Find the co-ordinates of a point on Y- axis which is equidistant from
M $(-5,-2)$ and N$(3,2)$
**Solution** : Let point P$(0, y)$ on Y- axis be equidistant from M$(-5,-2)$ and N$(3,2)$.
$$\therefore \text{PM} = \text{PN} \quad \therefore \text{PM}^2 = \text{PN}^2$$
$$\therefore [0 - (-5)]^2 + [y - (-2)]^2 = (0 - 3)^2 + (y - 2)^2$$
$$\therefore 25 + (y + 2)^2 = 9 + y^2 - 4y + 4$$
$$\therefore 25 + y^2 + 4y + 4 = 13 + y^2 - 4y$$
$$\therefore 8y = -16 \quad \therefore y = -2$$
$$\therefore \text{the co-ordinates of the point on the Y-axis which is equidistant from}$$
M and N are M $(0, -2)$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (6)** $A(-3, -4), B(-5, 0), C(3, 0)$ are the vertices of $\Delta$ ABC. Find the co-ordinates
of the circumcentre of $\Delta$ ABC.
**Solution** : Let, $P(a, b)$ be the circumcentre of $\Delta$ ABC.
$\therefore$ point $P$ is equidistant from A,B and C.
$\therefore PA^2 = PB^2 = PC^2 ......... (I) \quad \therefore PA^2 = PB^2$
$$(a + 3)^2 + (b + 4)^2 = (a + 5)^2 + (b - 0)^2$$
$$\therefore a^2 + 6a + 9 + b^2 + 8b + 16 = a^2 + 10a + 25 +b^2$$
$$\therefore -4a + 8b = 0$$
$$\therefore a - 2b = 0 ......... (II)$$
Similarly $PA^2 = PC^2 ......... (I)$ From
$$\therefore (a + 3)^2 + (b + 4)^2 = (a - 3)^2 + (b - 0)^2$$
$$\therefore a^2 + 6a + 9 + b^2 + 8b + 16 = a^2 - 6a + 9 + b^2$$
$$\therefore 12a + 8b = -16$$
$$\therefore 3a + 2b = -4 ......... (III)$$
Solving (II) and (III) we get $a = -1, b = -\frac{1}{2}$
$\therefore$ co-ordinates of circumcentre are $(-1, -\frac{1}{2})$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\textbf{Ex. (7)}   If point $(x, y)$ is equidistant from points $(7, 1)$ and $(3, 5)$, show that
$$y = x-2.$$
\textbf{Solution} : Let point P $(x, y)$ be equidistant from points A$(7, 1)$ and B$(3, 5)$
$$\therefore \text{AP} = \text{BP}$$
$$\therefore \text{AP}^2 = \text{BP}^2$$
$$\therefore (x - 7)^2 + (y - 1)^2 = (x - 3)^2 + (y - 5)^2$$
$$\therefore x^2 - 14x +49 + y^2 - 2y + 1 = x^2 - 6x + 9 + y^2 - 10y +25$$
$$\therefore - 8x + 8y = -16$$
$$\therefore x - y = 2$$
$$\therefore y = x - 2$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\textbf{Ex. (8)} Find the value of y if distance between points A $(2,-2)$ and B $(-1, y)$is 5.
\textbf{Solution} : $AB^2 = [(-1) - 2]^2 + [y - (-2)]^2 .........$ by distance formula
$\therefore \quad 5^2 = (-3)^2 + (y + 2)^2$
$\therefore \quad 25 = 9 + (y + 2)^2$
$\therefore \quad 16 = (y + 2)^2$
$\therefore \quad y + 2 = \pm\sqrt{16}$
$\therefore \quad y + 2 = \pm 4$
$\therefore \quad y = 4 - 2 \text{ or } y = -4 - 2$
$\therefore \quad y = 2 \quad \text{or} \quad y = -6$
$\therefore \text{value of } y \text{ is } 2 \text{ or } -6.$

**Ex. (1)** If A(3,5), B(7,9) and point Q divides seg AB in the ratio 2:3 then find

$$m : n = 2:3$$

$$x = \frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m + n} = \frac{2 \times 7 + 3 \times 3}{2 + 3} = \frac{23}{5} \qquad y = \frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m + n} = \frac{2 \times 9 + 3 \times 5}{2 + 3} = \frac{33}{5}$$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Remember this!

* Section formula
The co-ordinates of a point which divides the line segment joined by two distinct
points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ in the ratio $m : n$ are $\left(\frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m+n}, \frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m+n}\right)$.

* Midpoint formula
The co-ordinates of midpoint of a line segment joining two distinct points
$(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ are $\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right)$.

* Centroid formula
If $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)$ and $(x_3, y_3)$ are the vertices of a triangle then co-ordinates of
the centroid are $\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2 + x_3}{3}, \frac{y_1 + y_2 + y_3}{3}\right)$.

**Solution** : Let the co-ordinates of T be $(x, y)$.
$\therefore$ by the section formula,
$$x = \frac{mx_2 + nx_1}{m+n} = \frac{7 \times (-6) + 2 \times (-7)}{7+2}$$
$$= \frac{-42 - 14}{9} = \frac{-56}{9}$$
$$y = \frac{my_2 + ny_1}{m+n} = \frac{7 \times (-5) + 2 \times (4)}{7+2}$$
$$= \frac{-35 + 8}{9} = \frac{-27}{9} = -3$$
$\therefore$ co-ordinates of point T are $\left(\frac{-56}{9}, -3\right)$.

**Ex. (2)** If point $P(-4, 6)$ divides the line segment AB with $A(-6, 10)$ and $B(r, s)$ in
the ratio $2:1$, find the co-ordinates of $B$.

**Solution** : By section formula

$$ -4 = \frac{2 \times r + 1 \times (-6)}{2 + 1} \hspace{4em} 6 = \frac{2 \times s + 1 \times 10}{2 + 1} $$

$$ \therefore \quad -4 = \frac{2r - 6}{3} \hspace{10em} \therefore \quad 6 = \frac{2s + 10}{3} $$

$$ \therefore \quad -12 = 2r - 6 \hspace{10em} \therefore \quad 18 = 2s + 10 $$

$$ \therefore \quad 2r = -6 \hspace{12em} \therefore \quad 2s = 8 $$

$$ \therefore \quad r = -3 \hspace{12em} \therefore \quad s = 4 $$

$$ \therefore \text{ co-ordinates of point } B \text{ are } (-3, 4). $$

$x$ co-ordinate of point $P = \frac{1 \times (-7) + 2 \times 2}{1 + 2} = \frac{-7 + 4}{3} = \frac{-3}{3} = -1$

$y$ co-ordinate of point $P = \frac{1 \times 4 + 2 \times (-2)}{1 + 2} = \frac{4 - 4}{3} = \frac{0}{3} = 0$

Point $Q$ divides seg $AB$ in the ratio $2:1$. $\therefore \frac{AQ}{QD} = \frac{2}{1}$

$x$ co-ordinate of point $Q = \frac{2 \times (-7) + 1 \times 2}{2 + 1} = \frac{-14 + 2}{3} = \frac{-12}{3} = -4$

$y$ co-ordinate of point $Q = \frac{2 \times 4 + 1 \times -2}{2 + 1} = \frac{8 - 2}{3} = \frac{6}{3} = 2$

$\therefore$ co-ordinates of points of trisection are $(-1, 0)$ and $(-4, 2)$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ co-ordinates of points of trisection are $(-1, 0)$ and $(-4, 2)$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Slope of a line

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When we walk on a plane road we
need not exert much effort but while
climbing up a slope we need more effort.
In science, we have studied that while
climbing up a slope we have to work
against gravitational force.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In co-ordinate geometry, slope of
a line is an important concept. We will
learn it through the following activity.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From this activity, we understand that for any two points $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ on
line $l$, the ratio $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ is constant.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ are any two points on line $l$, the ratio $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$ is called the
slope of the line $l$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Generally slope is shown by letter $m$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \therefore \quad m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity II : In the figure, some points on

Now you will know,

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:

positive.
(2) Slope of line $n$ is negative.
(3) Slope of line $t$ is more than
slope of line $l$.
(4) Slopes of lines $l$ and $t$ which
make acute angles with X- axis,
are positive.
(5) Slope of line $n$ making obtuse angle with X- axis is negative.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Slopes of X-axis, Y-axis and lines parallel to axes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the figure 5.22, $(x_1, 0)$ and $(x_2, 0)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: are two points on the X- axis.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Slope of X- axis $= \frac{0 - 0}{x_2 - x_1} = 0$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the same way $(0, y_1)$ and $(0, y_2)$
are two points on the Y- axis.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Slope of Y- axis = $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{0 - 0} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{0}$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: But division by $0$ is not possible.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ slope of Y- axis can not be determined.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now try to find the slope of any line like line $m$ which is parallel to X- axis. It will
come out to be 0.
Similarly we cannot determine the slope of a line like line $l$ which is parallel to Y- axis

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Slope of line – using ratio in trigonometry

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the figure 5.23, points $\mathrm{P}(x_1, y_1)$ and $\mathrm{Q}(x_2, y_2)$ are on line $l$.
Line $l$ intersects X axis in point T.
seg QS $\perp$ X- axis, seg PR $\perp$ seg QS $\therefore$ seg PR $\parallel$ seg TS ......... corresponding
angle test

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\therefore \mathrm{QR} = y_2 - y_1 \text{ and } \mathrm{PR} = x_2 - x_1$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{QR}}{\mathrm{PR}}=\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}$ ......... (I)
Line TQ makes an angle $\theta$ with the X- axis .
$\therefore \quad \frac{\mathrm{QR}}{\mathrm{PR}}=\tan \theta$ ......... (II)
$\therefore \quad$ From (I) and (II), $\frac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}=\tan \theta$
$\therefore \quad m=\tan \theta$
Now $\operatorname{seg} \mathrm{PR} \| \operatorname{seg} \mathrm{TS}$, line $l$ is transversal
$\therefore \quad \angle \mathrm{QPR}=\angle \mathrm{QTS}$ ......corresponding
angles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From this, we can define slope in
another way. The tan ratio of an angle
made by the line with the positive direction
of X-axis is called the slope of that line.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When any two lines have same slope, these lines make equal angles with the
positive direction of X- axis.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ These two lines are parallel.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**EX. (1)** Find the slope of the line passing through the points A $(-3, 5)$, and B $(4, -1)$

**Solution** : Let, $x_1 = -3$, $x_2 = 4$, $y_1 = 5$, $y_2 = -1$

$\therefore$ Slope of line AB = $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{-1-5}{4-(-3)} = \frac{-6}{7}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**EX. (2)** Show that points $P(-2, 3)$, $Q(1, 2)$, $R(4, 1)$ are collinear.

**Solution** : $P(-2, 3)$, $Q(1, 2)$ and $R(4, 1)$ are given points

$$ \text{slope of line PQ} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{2-3}{1-(-2)} = -\frac{1}{3} $$

$$ \text{Slope of line QR} = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = \frac{1-2}{4-1} = -\frac{1}{3} $$

$$ \text{Slope of line PQ and line QR is equal.} $$

$$ \text{But point Q lies on both the lines.} $$

$$ \therefore \text{Point P, Q, R are collinear.} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ Point $P, Q, R$ are collinear.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\textbf{EX. (3)}   If slope of the line joining points P(k, 0) and Q(-3, -2) is $\frac{2}{7}$ then find $k$.

\textbf{Solution} : P(k, 0) and Q(-3, -2)

       Slope of line PQ = $\frac{-2-0}{-3-k} = \frac{-2}{-3-k}$

       But slope of line PQ is given to be $\frac{2}{7}$ .

       $\therefore \frac{-2}{-3-k} = \frac{2}{7} \quad \therefore k = 4$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**EX. (4)** If A (6, 1), B (8, 2), C (9, 4) and D (7, 3) are the vertices of $\square$ ABCD ,
show that $\square$ ABCD is a parallelogram.

**Solution** : You know that Slope of line = $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$

Slope of line AB = $\frac{2-1}{8-6} = \frac{1}{2}$ ......... (I)

Slope of line BC = $\frac{4-2}{9-8} = 2$ ......... (II)

Slope of line CD = $\frac{3-4}{7-9} = \frac{1}{2}$ ......... (III)

Slope of line DA = $\frac{3-1}{7-6} = 2$ ......... (IV)

Slope of line AB = Slope of line CD ......... From (I) and (III)
$\therefore$ line AB $\parallel$ line CD
Slope of line BC = Slope of line DA ......... From (II) and (IV)
$\therefore$ line BC $\parallel$ line DA
Both the pairs of opposite sides of the quadrilateral are parallel
$\therefore$ $\square$ ABCD is a parallelogram.

called “secant” and “cotangent” ratios respectively. They are written in brief as sec
and cot.

Remember this!

The relation between the trigonometric ratios,
according to the definitions of cosec, sec and cot ratios

$\bullet \quad \frac{1}{\sin \theta} = \text{cosec } \theta \quad \therefore \sin \theta \times \text{cosec } \theta = 1$

$\bullet \quad \frac{1}{\cos \theta} = \sec \theta \quad \therefore \cos \theta \times \sec \theta = 1$

$\bullet \quad \frac{1}{\tan \theta} = \cot \theta \quad \therefore \tan \theta \times \cot \theta = 1$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric identities

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the figure 6.3, $\Delta$ ABC is a right angled triangle, $\angle B = 90^\circ$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) $\sin\theta = \frac{BC}{AC}$
(ii) $\cos\theta = \frac{AB}{AC}$
(iii) $\tan\theta = \frac{BC}{AB}$
(iv) $\csc\theta = \frac{AC}{BC}$
(v) $\sec\theta = \frac{AC}{AB}$
(vi) $\cot\theta = \frac{AB}{BC}$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
By Pythagoras therom,
$$BC^2 + AB^2 = AC^2 \dots (I)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Dividing both the sides of (1) by $AC^2$
$$\frac{BC^2+AB^2}{AC^2} = \frac{AC^2}{AC^2}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \therefore \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} = 1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \therefore \left(\frac{\mathbf{BC}}{\mathbf{AC}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathbf{AB}}{\mathbf{AC}}\right)^2 = 1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\therefore (\sin\theta)^2 + (\cos\theta)^2 = 1 .... [(\sin\theta)^2 \text{ is written as } \sin^2\theta \text{ and } (\cos\theta)^2 \text{ is written}$
$\text{as } \cos^2\theta.]$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1 \dots \dots \dots \dots \text{ (II)} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now dividing both the sides of equation (II) by $\sin^2\theta$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{\sin^2 \theta} + \frac{\cos^2 \theta}{\sin^2 \theta} = \frac{1}{\sin^2 \theta} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{cot}^2 \theta = \mathbf{cosec}^2 \theta \dots\dots\dots (\mathrm{III}) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Dividing both the sides of equation (II) by $\cos^2\theta$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{\cos^2 \theta} + \frac{\cos^2 \theta}{\cos^2 \theta} = \frac{1}{\cos^2 \theta} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \tan^2 \theta + 1 = \sec^2 \theta $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathbf{1} + \mathbf{tan}^2\theta = \mathbf{sec}^2\theta \dots\dots\dots (\mathrm{IV}) $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Relations (II),(III), and (IV) are fundamental trigonometric identities.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Ex. (1) If $\sin\theta = \frac{20}{29}$ then find $\cos\theta$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (1) If $\sin\theta = \frac{20}{29}$ then find $\cos\theta$

**Solution : Method I**
We have
$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$
$\left(\frac{20}{29}\right)^2 + \cos^2\theta = 1$
$\frac{400}{841} + \cos^2\theta = 1$
$\cos^2\theta = 1 - \frac{400}{841}$
$= \frac{441}{841}$
Taking square root of
both sides.
$\cos\theta = \frac{21}{29}$

**Method II**
$\sin\theta = \frac{20}{29}$
from figure, $\sin\theta = \frac{AB}{AC}$
$\therefore AB = 20k$ and $AC = 29k$
Let $BC = x$.
According to Pythagoras therom,
$AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2$
$(20k)^2 + x^2 = (29k)^2$
$400k^2 + x^2 = 841k^2$
$x^2 = 841k^2 - 400k^2$
$= 441k^2$
$\therefore x = 21k$
$\therefore \cos\theta = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{21k}{29k} = \frac{21}{29}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (2) If $\sec\theta = \frac{25}{7}$, find the value of $\tan\theta$.
Solution : Method I                                                                                              Method II
we have ,                                                                                                                                  from the figure,
$$1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$$                                                                                              $\sec\theta = \frac{PR}{PQ}$
$\therefore$ $1 + \tan^2\theta = \left(\frac{25}{7}\right)^2$                                                                                              $\therefore$ $PQ = 7k$, $PR = 25k$
$\therefore$ $\tan^2\theta = \frac{625}{49} - 1$                                                                                                                                  According to Pythagoras therom,
                                                                                                                                                                                                $PQ^2 + QR^2 = PR^2$
                                                                                                                                                                                                $\therefore$ $(7k)^2 + QR^2 = (25k)^2$
                                                                                                                                                                                                $\therefore$ $QR^2 = 625k^2 - 49k^2 = 576k^2$
                                                                                                                                                                                                $\therefore$ $QR = 24k$
                                                                                                                                                                                                Now, $\tan\theta = \frac{QR}{PQ} = \frac{24k}{7k} = \frac{24}{7}$
$\therefore$ $\tan\theta = \frac{24}{7}$

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.5

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (3)** If $5\sin\theta - 12\cos\theta = 0$, find the values of $\sec\theta$ and $\text{cosec}\theta$.
**Solution :** $5\sin\theta - 12\cos\theta = 0$

$\therefore 5\sin\theta = 12\cos\theta$
$\therefore \frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \frac{12}{5}$
$\therefore \tan\theta = \frac{12}{5}$

we have,
$1 + \tan^2\theta = \sec^2\theta$
$\therefore 1 + \left(\frac{12}{5}\right)^2 = \sec^2\theta$

$\therefore 1 + \frac{144}{25} = \sec^2\theta$

$\therefore \frac{25+144}{25} = \sec^2\theta$

$\therefore \sec^2\theta = \frac{169}{25}$

$\therefore \sec\theta = \frac{13}{5}$

$\therefore \cos\theta = \frac{5}{13}$

Now, $\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta$

$\therefore \sin^2\theta = 1 - \cos^2\theta$

$\therefore \sin^2\theta = 1 - \left(\frac{5}{13}\right)^2$

$= 1 - \frac{25}{169}$

$= \frac{144}{169}$

$\therefore \sin\theta = \frac{12}{13}$

$\therefore \text{cosec}\theta = \frac{13}{12}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: **Ex. (4)** $\cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ then find the value of $\frac{1-\sec\theta}{1+\csc\theta}$

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : Method I

$$\cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \quad \therefore \sec\theta = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1$$
$$\therefore \sin^2\theta + \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2 = 1$$
$$\therefore \sin^2\theta = 1 - \frac{3}{4} = \frac{1}{4}$$
$$\therefore \sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \quad \therefore \text{cosec}\theta = 2$$
$$\therefore \frac{1-\sec\theta}{1+\text{cosec}\theta} = \frac{1-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}{1+2}$$
$$= \frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}-2}{\sqrt{3}}}{3}$$
$$= \frac{\sqrt{3}-2}{3\sqrt{3}}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (5) Show that $\sec x + \tan x = \sqrt{\frac{1 + \sin x}{1 - \sin x}}$

Solution : $\sec x + \tan x = \frac{1}{\cos x} + \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$

$= \frac{1 + \sin x}{\cos x}$

$= \sqrt{\frac{(1 + \sin x)^2}{\cos^2 x}}$

$= \sqrt{\frac{(1 + \sin x)(1 + \sin x)}{1 - \sin^2 x}}$

$= \sqrt{\frac{(1 + \sin x)(1 + \sin x)}{(1 - \sin x)(1 + \sin x)}}$

$= \sqrt{\frac{1 + \sin x}{1 - \sin x}}$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Method II

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

we know that, $\cos 30^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ .

$$\therefore \quad \theta = 30^\circ$$

$$\therefore \sec \theta = \sec 30^\circ = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$$

$$\text{cosec } \theta = \text{cosec } 30^\circ = 2$$

$$\therefore \frac{1-\sec\theta}{1+\text{cosec } \theta} = \frac{1-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}{1+2}$$

$$= \frac{\frac{\sqrt{3}-2}{\sqrt{3}}}{3}$$

$$= \frac{\sqrt{3}-2}{3\sqrt{3}}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (6)** Eliminate $\theta$ from given equations.
$$x = a \cot \theta - b \text{ cosec } \theta$$
$$y = a \cot \theta + b \text{ cosec } \theta$$

**Solution :**
$$x = a \cot \theta - b \text{ cosec } \theta \quad ......... \text{ (I)}$$
$$y = a \cot \theta + b \text{ cosec } \theta \quad ......... \text{ (II)}$$

Adding equations (I) and (II).
$$x + y = 2a \cot \theta$$
$$\therefore \cot \theta = \frac{x + y}{2a} \quad ......... \text{ (III)}$$

Subtracting equation (II) from (I) ,
$$y - x = 2b \text{ cosec } \theta$$
$$\therefore \text{cosec } \theta = \frac{y-x}{2b} \quad ......... \text{ (IV)}$$

Now, $\text{cosec}^2\theta - \cot^2\theta = 1$
$$\therefore \left(\frac{y-x}{2b}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{y+x}{2a}\right)^2 = 1$$
$$\therefore \frac{(y-x)^2}{4b^2} - \frac{(y+x)^2}{4a^2} = 1$$
$$\text{or } \left(\frac{y-x}{b}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{y+x}{a}\right)^2 = 4$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Application of trigonometry

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Many times we need to know
the height of a tower, building, tree or
distance of a ship from the lighthouse or
width of a river etc.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We cannot measure them actually
but we can find them with the help of
trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Paragraph
Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us study a few related terms.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
(i) Line of vision : If the observer is standing at the location ‘A’ ,looking at an object ‘B’
then the line AB is called line of the vision.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
**(ii) Angle of elevation :**
$\quad$ If an observer at A, observes the
point B which is at a level higher than A
and AM is the horizontal line, then
$\angle$ BAM is called the angle of elevation.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.7

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: (iii) Angle of depression :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If an observer at A, observes the
point C which is at a level lower than
A and AM is the horizontal line, the
$\angle$ MAC is called the angle of depression.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.8

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When we see above the horizontal line, the angle formed is the angle of elevation.
When we see below the horizontal line, the angle formed is the angle of depression.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** An observer at a distance of 10 m from a tree looks at the top of the tree, the
angle of elevation is $60^{\circ}$. What is the height of the tree ? ($\sqrt{3}$ = 1.73)
**Solution :** In figure 6.9, AB = h = height of the tree.
BC = 10 m, distance of the observer from the tree .
Angle of elevation ($\theta$) = $\angle$ BCA = $60^{\circ}$
from figure, $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}}$ ......... (I)
$\tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3}$ ......... (II)
$\therefore \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}} = \sqrt{3}$ ......... from equation (I)and (II)
$\therefore \text{AB} = \text{BC} \sqrt{3} = 10 \sqrt{3}$
$\therefore \text{AB} = 10 \times 1.73 = 17.3 \text{ m}$
$\therefore \text{height of the tree is } 17.3\text{m}$.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 6.9

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (2)** From the top of a building, an observer is looking at a scooter parked
at some distance away, makes an angle of depression of $30^{\circ}$.
If the height of the building is 40m, find how far the scooter is from the
building. ($\sqrt{3} = 1.73$)
**Solution:** In the figure 6.10, AB is the
building. A scooter is at C
which is ‘x’ m away from the
building.
In figure, ‘A’ is the position of
the observer.
AM is the horizontal line and $\angle$ MAC is the angle of depression.
$\angle$ MAC and $\angle$ ACB are alternate angles.
from fig, $\tan30^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{BC}$
$\therefore \quad \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{40}{x}$
$\therefore \quad x = 40\sqrt{3}$
$= 40 \times 1.73$
$= 69.20 \text{ m.}$
$\therefore$ the scooter is 69.20 m. away from the building.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (3) To find the width of the river, a man observes the top of a tower on the
opposite bank making an angle of elevation of $61^{\circ}$. When he moves 50m
backword from bank and observes the same top of the tower, his line
of vision makes an angle of elevation of $35^{\circ}$. Find the
height of the tower and width of the river. $(\tan 61^{\circ} = 1.8, \tan 35^{\circ} = 0.7)$

Solution : seg AB shows the tower on
the opposite bank. 'A' is the top of
the tower and seg BC shows the
width of the river. Let '$h$' be the
height of the tower and '$x$' be the
width of the river.
from figure, $\tan 61^{\circ} = \frac{h}{x}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\therefore 1.8 = \frac{h}{x}$
$h = 1.8 \times x$
$10h = 18x$ ......... (I)...... multiplying by 10
In right angled $\Delta$ ABD,
$\tan 35 = \frac{h}{x + 50}$
$0.7 = \frac{h}{x + 50}$
$\therefore \quad h = 0.7 (x + 50)$
$\therefore \quad 10h = 7 (x + 50)$ ......... (II)
$\therefore$ from equations (I) and (II) ,
$18x = 7(x + 50)$
$\therefore 18x = 7x + 350$
$\therefore 11x = 350$
$\therefore \quad x = \frac{350}{11} = 31.82$
Now, $h = 1.8x = 1.8 \times 31.82$
$= 57.28$ m.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ width of the river $= 31.82$ m and height of tower $= 57.28$ m

blocks.label: Question
blocks.text:
Ex. (4)   Roshani saw an eagle on the
top of a tree at an angle of
elevation of $61^{\circ}$, while she was
standing at the door of her
house. She went on the terrace
of the house so that she could
see it clearly. The terrace
was at a height of $4m$. While
observing the eagle from there
theangleofelevationwas$52^{\circ}$.At
whatheight from the ground was
the eagle ?
(Find the answer correct upto
nearest integer)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Solution :** In figure 6.12, PQ is the house and SR is the tree. The eagle is at R.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Draw seg QT $\perp$ seg RS.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore \square$ TSPQ is a rectangle.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Let SP = $x$ and TR = $y$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now in $\Delta$ RSP, $\angle$ PRS $= 90^{\circ} - 61^{\circ} = 29^{\circ}$

and in $\Delta$ RTQ, $\angle$ QRT $= 90^{\circ} - 52^{\circ} = 38^{\circ}$

$\therefore \tan \angle$ PRS $= \tan 29^{\circ} = \frac{\text{SP}}{\text{RS}}$

$\therefore 0.55 = \frac{x}{y + 4}$

$\therefore x = 0.55(y + 4)$ ......... (I)

Similarly, $\tan \angle$ QRT $= \frac{\text{TQ}}{\text{RT}}$

$\therefore \tan 38^{\circ} = \frac{x}{y}$ ......... [$\because$ SP = TQ = $x$]

$\therefore 0.78 = \frac{x}{y}$

$\therefore x = 0.78y$ ......... (II)

$\therefore 0.78y = 0.55(y + 4)$ ......... from (I) and (II)

$\therefore 78y = 55(y + 4)$

$\therefore 78y = 55y + 220$

$\therefore 23y = 220$

$\therefore y = 9.565 = 10$ (upto nearest integer)

$\therefore \text{RS} = y + 4 = 10 + 4 = 14$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ the eagle was at a height of 14 metre from the ground.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (5)** A tree was broken due to storm. Its broken upper part was so inclined that
its top touched the ground making an angle of $30^{\circ}$with the ground.The
distance from the foot of the tree and the point where the top touched the
ground was 10 metre. What was the height of the tree.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution:** As shown in figure 6.13, suppose AB is the tree. It was broken at ‘C’ and its
top touched at ‘D’.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\angle \text{CDB} = 30^{\circ}, \text{BD} = 10 \text{ m}, \text{BC} = x \text{ m}$
$\text{CA} = \text{CD} = y \text{ m}$
In right angled $\Delta \text{CDB},$
$$\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{BD}}$$
$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{x}{10}$$
$$x = \frac{10}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$y = \frac{20}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$x + y = \frac{10}{\sqrt{3}} + \frac{20}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$= \frac{30}{\sqrt{3}}$$
$$x + y = 10\sqrt{3}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ height of the tree was $10\sqrt{3}$ m.

blocks.text: 5. Prove the following.

blocks.label: List

(1) $\sec\theta (1 - \sin\theta) (\sec\theta + \tan\theta) = 1$
(2) $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta) (1 - \sin\theta) = \cos\theta$
(3) $\sec^2\theta + \text{cosec}^2\theta = \sec^2\theta \times \text{cosec}^2\theta$

$l$		 Lateral surface area = $4l^2$

$h$		 Curved surface area = $2\pi rh$

$h$		 Slant height ( $l$ ) = $\sqrt{h^2 + r^2}$

Volume = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3
6. Hemisphere Curved surface area = 2\pi r^2

Volume = \frac{2}{3} \pi r^3

blocks.label: Paragraph

As shown in the above figures, take a ball and a beaker of the same radius as that
of the ball. Cut a strip of paper of length equal to the diameter of the beaker. Draw
two lines on the strip dividing it into three equal parts. Stick it on the beaker straight
up from the bottom. Fill water in the beaker upto the first mark of the strip from the
bottom. Push the ball in the beaker slowly so that it touches its bottom. Observe how
much the water level rises.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You will notice that the water level has risen exactly upto the total height of the strip.
Try to understand how we get the formula for the volume of a the sphere. The shape
of the beaker is cylindrical.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, the volume of the part of the beaker upto height $2r$ can be obtained by
the formula of volume of a cylinder. Let us assume that the volume is $V$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \therefore V = \pi r^2 h = \pi \times r^2 \times 2r = 2\pi r^3 \qquad (\because h = 2r) $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
But $V =$ volume of the ball $+$ volume of the water which was already in the beaker.
$= \text{volume of the ball} + \frac{1}{3} \times 2\pi r^3$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\therefore$ volume of the ball $= V - \frac{1}{3} \times 2\pi r^3$
$= 2\pi r^3 - \frac{2}{3} \pi r^3$
$= \frac{6\pi r^3 - 2\pi r^3}{3} = \frac{4\pi r^3}{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence we get the formula of the volume of a sphere as $V = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3$

**Ex. (1)**   The radius and height of a cylindrical water reservoir is 2.8 m and 3.5 m
respectively. How much maximum water can the tank hold ? A person needs
70 litre of water per day. For how many persons is the water sufficient for
a day ? ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$)

**Solution :** (r) = 2.8 m,   ( h) = 3.5 m, $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$
Capacity of the water reservoir = Volume of the cylindrical reservoir
$$= \pi r^2 h$$
$$= \frac{22}{7} \times 2.8 \times 2.8 \times 3.5$$
$$= 86.24 \text{ m}^3$$
$$= 86.24 \times 1000 \quad (\because 1m^3 = 1000 \text{ litre})$$
$$= 86240.00 \text{ litre}.$$

$\therefore$ the reservoir can hold 86240 litre of water.

The daily requirement of water of a person is 70 litre.

$\therefore$ water in the tank is sufficient for $\frac{86240}{70} = 1232$ persons.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (2)** How many solid cylinders of radius 10 cm and height 6 cm can be made by
melting a solid sphere of radius 30 cm ?
**Solution :** Radius of a sphere, $r = 30$ cm
Radius of the cylinder, $R = 10$ cm
Height of the cylinder, $H = 6$ cm
Let the number of cylinders be $n$.
Volume of the sphere $= n \times$ volume of a cylinder
$$\therefore n = \frac{\text{Volume of the sphere}}{\text{Volume of a cylinder}}$$
$$= \frac{\frac{4}{3} \pi (r)^3}{\pi (R)^2 H}$$
$$= \frac{\frac{4}{3} \times (30)^3}{10^2 \times 6} = \frac{\frac{4}{3} \times 30 \times 30 \times 30}{10 \times 10 \times 6} = 60$$
$\therefore$ 60 cylinders can be made .

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ 60 cylinders can be made .

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (3)** A tent of a circus is such that its lower part is cylindrical and upper part
is conical. The diameter of the base of the tent is 48 m and the height of the
cylindrical part is 15 m. Total height of the tent is 33 m. Find area
of canvas required to make the tent. Also find volume of air in the tent.
**Solution :** Total height of the tent = 33 m.
Let height of the cylindrical part be H
$\therefore$ H = 15 m.
Let the height of the conical part be h
$\therefore h = (33-15) = 18$ m.
Slant height of cone, $l = \sqrt{r^2 + (h)^2}$
$$= \sqrt{24^2 + 18^2}$$
$$= \sqrt{576 + 324}$$
$$= \sqrt{900}$$
$$= 30$ m.
Canvas required for tent = Curved surface area of the cylindrical part +
Curved surface area of conical part
$$= 2\pi r \text{H} + \pi r l$$
$$= \pi r (2 \text{H} + l)$$
$$= \frac{22}{7} \times 24 (2 \times 15 + 30)$$
$$= \frac{22}{7} \times 24 \times 60$$
$$= 4525.71 \text{ m}^2$$
Volume of air in the tent = volume of cylinder + volume of cone
$$= \pi r^2 \text{H} + \frac{1}{3} \pi r^2 h$$
$$= \pi r^2 \left( \text{H} + \frac{1}{3} h \right)$$
$$= \frac{22}{7} \times 24^2 (15 + \frac{1}{3} \times 18)$$
$$= \frac{22}{7} \times 576 \times 21$$
$$= 38,016 \text{ m}^3$$
$\therefore$ canvas required for the tent = $4525.71 \text{ m}^2$
$\therefore$ volume of air in the tent = $38,016 \text{ m}^3$.

blocks.label: Infobox

Remember this!

$h =$ height of a frustum, $l =$ slant height height of a frustum,
$r_1$ and $r_2 =$ radii of circular faces of a frustum ( $r_1 > r_2$ )
Slant height of a frustum $= l = \sqrt{h^2 + (r_1 - r_2)^2}$
Curved surface area of a frustum $= \pi l ( r_1 + r_2 )$
Total surface area of a frustum $= \pi l (r_1 + r_2) + \pi r_1^2 + \pi r_2^2$
Volume of a frustum $= \frac{1}{3} \pi h (r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_1 \times r_2)$

**Ex. (1)** A bucket is frustum shaped. Its height is 28 cm. Radii of circular faces are
12 cm and 15 cm. Find the capacity of the bucket. ( $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ )

**Solution :** $r_1 = 15$ cm, $r_2 = 12$ cm, h = 28 cm
Capacity of the bucket = Volume of frustum
$$= \frac{1}{3} \pi h ( r_1^2 + r_2^2 + r_1 \times r_2)$$
$$= \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{22}{7} \times 28 (15^2 \times 12^2 + 15 \times 12)$$
$$= \frac{22 \times 4}{3} \times (225 + 144 + 180)$$
$$= \frac{22 \times 4}{3} \times 549$$
$$= 88 \times 183$$
$$= 16104 \text{ cm}^3 = 16.104 \text{ litre}$$
$\therefore$ capacity of the bucket is 16.104 litre.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (2)** Radii of the top and the base of a frustum are 14 cm, 8 cm respectively. Its
height is 8 cm. Find its
i) curved surface area      ii) total surface area      iii) volume.

**Solution :** $r_1 = 14 \text{ cm}$ , $r_2 = 8 \text{ cm}$, $h = 8 \text{ cm}$

Slant height of the frustum $= l = \sqrt{h^2 + (r_1 - r_2)^2}$
$= \sqrt{8^2 + (14 - 8)^2}$
$= \sqrt{64 + 36} = 10 \text{ cm}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Curved surface area of the frustum $= \pi(\mathrm{r}_{1}+\mathrm{r}_{2}) l$
$=3.14 \times(14+8) \times 10$
$=690.8 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$
Total surface area of frustum $=\pi l(\mathrm{r}_{1}+\mathrm{r}_{2})+\pi \mathrm{r}_{1}^{2}+\pi \mathrm{r}_{2}^{2}$
$=3.14 \times 10(14+8)+3.14 \times 14^{2}+3.14 \times 8^{2}$
$=690.8+615.44+200.96$
$=690.8+816.4$
$=1507.2 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$
Volume of the frustum $=\frac{1}{3} \pi \mathrm{h}\left(\mathrm{r}_{1}^{2}+\mathrm{r}_{2}^{2}+\mathrm{r}_{1} \times \mathrm{r}_{2}\right)$
$=\frac{1}{3} \times 3.14 \times 8\left(14^{2}+8^{2}+14 \times 8\right)$
$=3114.88 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$

The pattern in the above table shows that, if measure of an arc of a circle is $\theta$, then

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: From the formula, $\frac{l}{2\pi r} = \frac{\theta}{360}$

blocks.label: Equation

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: A relation between length of an arc and area of the sector

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Area of a sector, (A) = $\frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$ ......... I

Length of an arc, (l) = $\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$

$\therefore \frac{\theta}{360} = \frac{l}{2\pi r}$ ......... II

$\therefore A = \frac{l}{2\pi r} \times \pi r^2$ .........From I and II

$A = \frac{1}{2} l r = \frac{l r}{2}$

$\therefore$ Area of a sector = $\frac{\text{Length of the arc} \times \text{Radius}}{2}$

Similarly, $\frac{A}{\pi r^2} = \frac{l}{2\pi r} = \frac{\theta}{360}$

blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** The measure of a central angle of
a circle is $150^{\circ}$ and radius of the
circle is $21$ cm. Find the length of
the arc and area of the sector
associated with the central angle.

**Solution :** $r = 21$ cm, $\theta = 150$, $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$

Area of the sector, A $= \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$
$= \frac{150}{360} \times \frac{22}{7} \times 21 \times 21$
$= \frac{1155}{2} = 577.5$ cm$^2$

Length of the arc, $l = \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$

$= \frac{150}{360} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 21$
$= 55$ cm

\textbf{ex. (2)}      In figure 7.29, P is the centre of the

$$(\sqrt{3} = 1.73)$$

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
**Solution** Radius joining point of contact of the tangent is perpendicular to the tangent.
$\therefore$ in $\Delta$ PQR, $\angle$ PQR $= 90^{\circ}$,      PQ $= 6$ cm, PR $= 12$ cm $\therefore$ PQ $= \frac{\text{PR}}{2}$
If one side of a right anglesd triangle is half the hypoteneus then angle
opposite to, that side is of $30^{\circ}$ measure
$\therefore$ $\angle$ R $= 30^{\circ}$ and $\angle$ P $= 60^{\circ}$
$\therefore$ by $30^{\circ}$-$60^{\circ}$-$90^{\circ}$ theorem, $\text{QR} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times \text{PR} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 12 = 6\sqrt{3}$
$\therefore$ QR $= 6\sqrt{3}$ cm
$\therefore$ A($\Delta$ PQR) $= \frac{1}{2}$ QR $\times$ PQ
$$= \frac{1}{2} \times 6\sqrt{3} \times 6$$
$$= 18\sqrt{3} = 18 \times 1.73$$
$$= 31.14 \text{ cm}^2$$
Area of a sector $= \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$
$$A(P-QAB) = \frac{60}{360} \times 3.14 \times 6^2$$
$$= \frac{1}{6} \times 3.14 \times 6 \times 6 = 3.14 \times 6$$
$$= 18.84 \text{ cm}^2$$
Area of shaded region $= A(PQR) - A(P-QAB)$
$$= 31.14 - 18.84$$
$$= 12.30 \text{ cm}^2$$
Area of the shaded region $= 12.30 \text{ cm}^2$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Segment of a circle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Segment of a circle is the region bounded by a chord and
its corresponding arc of the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Minor segment :** The area enclosed by a chord and its corresponding minor arc is
called a minor segment. In the figure, segment AXB is a minor
segment.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Major segment :** The area enclosed by a chord and its corresponding major arc is
called a major segment. In the figure, seg AYB is a major segment.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Semicircular segment :** A segment formed by a diameter of a circle is called a
semicircular segment.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
\textbf{Ex. (1)} \quad In the figure 7.40, $\angle$ AOB $= 30^{\circ}$,
OA $= 12$ cm . Find the area of
the segment. $(\pi = 3.14)$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Method I**

$$r = 12, \quad \theta = 30^\circ, \quad \pi = 3.14$$

$$A(O-AXB) = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$$

$$= \frac{30}{360} \times 3.14 \times 12^2$$

$$= 3.14 \times 12$$

$$= 37.68 \text{ cm}^2$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$A(\Delta \text{ OAB}) = \frac{1}{2} \text{ r}^2 \times \sin\theta$$
$$= \frac{1}{2} \times 12^2 \times \sin 30$$
$$= \frac{1}{2} \times 144 \times \frac{1}{2}$$
$$.....(\because \sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2})$$
$$= 36 \text{ cm}^2$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{A}(\text{segment AXB}) &= \mathrm{A} (\mathrm{O} - \mathrm{AXB}) - \mathrm{A}(\Delta \mathrm{OAB}) \\
&= 37.68 - 36 \\
&= 1.68 \mathrm{~cm}^2
\end{aligned}
$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Method II

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{A(segment AXB)} &= r^2 \left[ \frac{\pi\theta}{360} - \frac{\sin\theta}{2} \right] \\
&= 12^2 \left[ \frac{3.14 \times 30}{360} - \frac{\sin 30}{2} \right] \\
&= 144 \left[ \frac{3.14}{12} - \frac{1}{2 \times 2} \right] \\
&= \frac{144}{4} \left[ \frac{3.14}{3} - 1 \right] \\
&= 36 \left[ \frac{3.14 - 3}{3} \right] \\
&= \frac{36}{3} \times 0.14 \\
&= 12 \times 0.14 \\
&= 1.68 \text{ cm}^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (2)**   The radius of a circle with centre P is 10 cm. If chord AB of the circle
substends a right angle at P, find areas of the minor segment and the major
segment. ($\pi = 3.14$)
**Solution :**      $r = 10$ cm, $\theta = 90$, $\pi = 3.14$
$A(P-AXB) = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$
$= \frac{90}{360} \times 3.14 \times 10^2$
$= \frac{1}{4} \times 314$
$= 78.5 \text{ cm}^2$
$A(\Delta APB) = \frac{1}{2} \text{ base} \times \text{height}$
$= \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 10$
$= 50 \text{ cm}^2$
$A \text{ (minor segment)} = A(P-AXB) - A(\Delta PAB)$
$= 78.5 - 50$
$= 28.5 \text{ cm}^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$
\begin{aligned}
A(\text{major segment}) &= A(\text{circle}) - A(\text{minor segment}) \\
&= 3.14 \times 10^2 - 28.5 \\
&= 314 - 28.5 \\
&= 285.5 \text{ cm}^2
\end{aligned}
$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (3)   A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius 14 cm. Find the area of
the region between the circle and the hexagon.          ($\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ , $\sqrt{3} = 1.732$)

Solution : side of the hexagon = 14 cm
$A(\text{hexagon}) = 6 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times (\text{side})^2$
$= 6 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 14^2$
$= 509.208 \text{ cm}^2$
$A(\text{circle}) = \pi r^2$
$= \frac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14$
$= 616 \text{ cm}^2$

The area of the region between the circle and the hexagon
$= A(\text{circle}) - A(\text{hexagon})$
$= 616 - 509.208$
$= 106.792 \text{ cm}^2$

11. In the figure 7.48, square ABCD is
inscribed in the sector A-PCQ. The
radius of sector C-BXD is 20 cm.
Complete the following activity
to find the area of shaded region.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
**Solution :** Side of square ABCD = radius of sector C - BXD = $\text{\textcircled{1}}$ cm
Area of square = (side)$^2$ = $\text{\textcircled{1}}^2$ = $\text{\textcircled{1}}$ ..... (I)
Area of shaded region inside the square
= Area of square ABCD - Area of sector C - BXD
= $\text{\textcircled{1}} - \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$
= $\text{\textcircled{1}} - \frac{90}{360} \times \frac{3.14}{1} \times \frac{400}{1}$
= $\text{\textcircled{1}} - 314$
= $\text{\textcircled{1}}$

Radius of bigger sector = Length of diagonal of square ABCD
= $20\sqrt{2}$
Area of the shaded regions outside the square
= Area of sector A - PCQ - Area of square ABCD
= A(A - PCQ) - A($\square$ABCD)
= $\left(\frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi \times r^2\right) - \text{\textcircled{1}}^2$
= $\frac{90}{360} \times 3.14 (20\sqrt{2})^2 - (20)^2$
= $\text{\textcircled{1}} - \text{\textcircled{1}}$
= $\text{\textcircled{1}}$

$\therefore$ total area of the shaded region = $86 + 228 = 314$ sq.cm.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ total area of the shaded region $= 86 + 228 = 314$ sq.cm.
